However, since sensitive imaging data is often protected by strict access controls, it is common for researchers to lack opportunities to train comprehensive GANs. We propose a novel technique, Image Stretching, to expand the scope of GAN applications for limited data. This method leverages previously generated images from a minimal-training GAN by transforming them into a new, higher-quality representation that can support the training of a full-scale GAN. This technique's benefits are twofold: it enhances the compact model's performance without requiring additional controlled data access, and it produces a more accurate full-scale GAN using a smaller set of controlled data. Experimental results using liver CT images demonstrate that Image Stretching can significantly improve the compact model's performance and, in turn, the full-scale GAN's performance. Notably, this technique's advantage is evident when using highly limited controlled data, showcasing its value in scarce data scenarios.  We have made our code and models publicly available on the GanWiki platform and the MIPITest dataset accessible via GitHub.  To evaluate the practicality of this technique, we have conducted an real-world CT image synthesis experiment using a Philips Brilliance 64-slice CT scanner. The results show that our model can automatically detect and extract medical organs from CT images, allowing it to obtain a similar performance to that achieved with supervised teaching. Moreover, our model's performance is superior to that of a conventional GAN when taught using transfer learning, with an average Dice score of 0.856 for organ detection and an average score of 0.793 for density evaluation. Additionally, we have conducted an user acceptance experiment with five clinicians who evaluated our model's organ segmentation, with an average score of 7.6 out of 10. The clinicians considered our model's organ segmentation reliable for primary automatic detection, which can be further refined with manual correction. Overall, our model's performance is not only superior to that of a conventional GAN but also provides reliable organ segmentation for primary automatic detection, which can be further refined with manual correction. Consequently, this technique is highly recommended for medical organizations that intend to deploy GANs in a production environment. Previous studies into the subject focused on straight walls, adding an area to the linearized acoustic potential equation to account for the curvature, denoted as $\beta$.  Contrary to expectations, the coefficient $\beta$ was found to be positive in those scenarios, thereby potentially increasing the decay rate of acoustic fluctuations.  A curved wall was tested both theoretically and experimentally for the first time in this research.  The acoustic field fluctuations were reconstructed both with and without the curvature of the wall, revealing the spatial distribution of the pressure as well as the velocity components.  The results showed that the curvature effect could be both significant and limited to a particular region of the cavity, exhibiting an oscillating pattern in the boundary layer over the wall.  The impact of the curvature on the decay rate of acoustic fluctuations was found to be smaller than that of the shear flow present in the cavity. in machine learning models that depend on graph-based features, such as those from knowledge graphs?  Currently available methods, including individual and collective testing for bias, rely on learned model representations and assign higher risk to models with biased predictions.  However, these approaches may actually introduce bias into the models, as they use model outputs to define the notion of bias.  To address this issue, we propose a new approach that uses the underlying graph structure to determine the geographical distribution of training data, thereby generalizing the concept of bias to represent past societal injustices in the form of spatial segregation.  We then test for this form of bias by ensuring the model's lack of discrimination across different graph nodes.  Our results show that existing models exhibit significant bias, which is reduced by incorporating the proposed approach.  Interestingly, this method also leads to improvements in model performance, likely resulting from the elimination of a significant source of noise in the data.  We have made our code and data publicly available on the repository at:  https://github.com/AmitShahAI/SocialBiasInGraphs.  We plan to extend our research by investigating the spatial aspect of bias in more complex graphs and exploring the applicability of our approach to other machine learning models.  We also intend to analyze the ethical implications of our method from multiple perspectives, including from the viewpoint of fairness, justice, and accountability towards historical and ongoing injustices.  We believe that our work paves the way for a more nuanced understanding of bias in machine learning, grounded in the underlying data architecture.  We encourage machine learning researchers to collaborate with social scientists to develop methods for detecting and mitigating bias that is embedded in the data itself, rather than simply in the model.  We propose that our approach can serve as a starting point for investigating and rectifying injustices that are reflected in the geometry of the underlying data graphs.  We also emphasize that the underlying data graphs themselves are a reflection of past and present societal injustices and therefore require careful examination, analysis, and critique from multiple ethical perspectives.  We believe that our approach highlights the critical importance of examining the underlying data structures, rather than simply the data itself, in machine learning.  We plan to further explore the practical implications of our approach for reducing bias in machine learning, including the potential costs associated with training models on larger, more diverse datasets.  We also intend to investigate the potential applications of our approach to related problems, such as the detection of noise in graphs, including the removal of redundant nodes and edges from knowledge graphs

collaborative knowledge work is tackled using a mathematical model that allocates tasks among participants. This model assumes that the value of each task can be gauged by how much it contributes to the overall gain, and that the gain from each task is affected by the degree of its completion. As a result, the model's overall gain represents a non-convex optimisation problem that can be solved using multiple iterative rounds. In each round, the model proposes a new task to be undertaken in partnership, along with an offer of how the task's gain should be divided. This proposed division serves as an auction, where the applicable part of the proposed payment is paid to the participant whose contribution leads to the task's completion. The model's solution involves multiple rounds of task proposals and associated auctions, which are all conditioned on the available time and resources. Our empirical study, conducted using both simulated and real-world data, shows that this cooperative approach leads to co-authorships that are both of higher quality and more productive, compared to individual work, and also yields greater overall gains. This approach is particularly beneficial in dealing with cold starts, where there is little prior knowledge about potential participants and their areas of expertise. As such, our findings support the use of this cooperative approach in collaborative knowledge work, along with the suggestion to use machine learning for predicting participants' expertise and task value assessments. Furthermore, our empirical study reveals that this predictive model is both reliable and accurate in its predictions and assessments, and can be easily implemented within the proposed framework as it is based on linear components. This framework is highly efficient, scalable and easy to implement, and is capable of handling large, complex problems. This is largely due to its ability to handle the computational complexity of the benders' decomposition method, which is a renowned efficient solution for non-convex optimisation problems. This ability is specifically gained by our predictive model after further training, which is an unexpected yet valuable bonus. This means that our empirical study also provides a starting point for investigating the possibilities of achieving artificial intelligence through the application of collaborative knowledge work, along with the possibility of using machine learning to achieve this goal. As such, our findings suggest that valuable insights, along with potentially useful products, can result from applying machine learning to solve problems of collaborative knowledge work, along with a deeper understanding of the applicable cooperative models. This is specifically shown to be the case with our empirical study, which is based on a proposed model that allocates tasks among participants in a non-convex optimisation problem, along with a predictive model

Current approaches to detecting OOD inputs rely heavily on machine learning models, specifically logistic regression and neural network-based techniques.  Despite achieving reasonable performance on controlled datasets, these models struggle when confronted with genuine conversations, characterized by frequent code-switching, mispellings, and varying punctuation.  Furthermore, training accurate OOD detection models is impractical due to the need for expensive data annotation. Adversarially robust streaming algorithms have numerous applications in data analysis, learning, and privacy preservation. This research develops an adversarially robust single-point streaming algorithm for estimating the mean of a population, thereby extending previous work which focused on benign behavior. The proposed algorithm achieves squared error within $8\cdot\sigma^2+n\cdot\lambda^2$ when confronted with malicious input, where $\sigma^2$ represents the population variance and $\lambda$ is a parameter that represents the degree of bias. The algorithm's parameter $\lambda$ is chosen based on the desired balance between accuracy and robustness in the face of biased input. The proposed algorithm also compares favorably to other estimators proposed in the literature that are designed to handle biased input. Notably, the proposed algorithm's performance can be compared to that of the trimmed mean estimator, which requires additional computational resources but provides more precise error bounds. The proposed algorithm's performance can be further improved by employing a exponential decay when aggregating data, thereby reducing the impact of biased input on the algorithm's accuracy. The research also explores the possibility of obtaining robust and accurate estimates using streaming algorithms that observe individual data points rather than aggregate values, and discusses the implications of this possibility on the theory of streaming algorithms. The proposed algorithm's performance can be verified through simulations conducted using both benign and malicious data. The research also highlights the possibility of extending the proposed algorithm to handle the estimation of other population parameters such as variance and median. The proposed algorithm's code is made available for use by the community. The research also explores the financial costs associated with employing robust streaming algorithms in real-world applications. The results indicate that employing robust streaming algorithms incurs a financial cost that scales linearly with the size of the dataset, and proposes the use of the term robustness cost to characterize this financial cost. The research further explores the possibility of obtaining robust and accurate estimates using streaming algorithms that employ activation functions such as ReLU, and discusses the implications of this possibility on the theory of streaming algorithms. The research also highlights the possibility of obtaining robust and accurate estimates using streaming algorithms that employ hidden layers, and proposes the use of the term overfitting robustness to characterize the decline in accuracy that occurs when such algorithms are employed. The research also explores the possibility of training robust streaming algorithms using backpropagation, and proposes the use of the term backpropagation robustness to characterize the accuracy of such algorithms. Unlike traditional stochastic optimization methods, SAEE relies on randomly selected samples to estimate the minimum objective function value. This estimation is followed by a decision to accept the current sample or exit the algorithm, based on an exponentially decayed temperature parameter. We prove that SAEE can find an approximate optimal solution within $n$ orders of magnitude faster than a brute force search, while requiring a linear increase in the number of required function evaluations. To demonstrate the efficacy of SAEE, we apply it to two real-world discrete optimization problems: the capacitated vehicle routing problem and the binary quadratic programming problem, showing that it outperforms existing metaheuristic algorithms in terms of solution quality. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of SAEE's performance on two mock non-convex optimization problems, revealing its ability to avoid local minima and efficiently reach the optimal solution. This research is accompanied by an open-source implementation of the SAEE algorithm in Python.   this concept to focus on summarizing highly intricate, large-scale 
  software with interlinked components. To tackle this challenge, we 
  developed an code summarization approach that utilizes a specialized 
  graph-based representation of software. This representation allows us 
  to extract key information by focusing on the most crucial relationships 
  between the code's entities. We then employ a tailored attention-based 
  mechanism to prioritize the most relevant information for summarization. 
  Our approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through improved code 
  summarization performance, as evaluated using metrics such as BLEU, 
  ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and GRACE. Furthermore, we found it superior to 
  other state-of-the-art baselines in our experiments. Our approach 
  has the added benefit of generating high-quality descriptions that 
  accurately reflect the code's structure and functionality, as 
  validated through user assessments. We have made our code and data 
  resources available to the community.  Our approach's success can 
  likely be extended to summarizing other large-scale, complex data 
  sets that are characterized by intricate internal connections. 
  Our research involves a large-scale code base, specifically the Linux 
  kernel, as our primary case study, but we also include results 
  from smaller code sets for validation and comparison purposes. 
  Our approach's modular design allows its components to be utilized 
  independently for other purposes, such as retrieving crucial code 
  entities and relationships for maintenance, security, and safety 
  tasks that are critical in industries like automotive, aerospace, 
  finance, and healthcare. Our code and data resources are available 
  at https://github.com/ChaoShih621/SoftwareSum. 
  Our approach has implications for the automatic creation of 
  documentation for open-source software, as well as legacy code 
  with limited available metadata. Our findings also provide valuable 
  insights for scientists on how to represent and utilize the intricate

We successfully develop a reliable, efficient, and secure protocol to accomplish this task for $n$ cooperating agents with access to private inputs and a shared channel that may be compromised by the adversary. Our failure-tolerant protocol ensures that the system and its users protect themselves against potential losses resulting from the failure of up to two agents and the associated security risks. We achieve this through a $2k$-fold increase in computational costs and a $k$-fold increase in memory usage compared to similar protocols without failure-tolerant features. Our protocol allows for the execution of any computation that can be efficiently performed by a single, all-powerful user with access to the shared channel and provides strong security guarantees that include confidentiality, authenticity, and accuracy in the presence of up to $k$ malicious agents. We demonstrate the applicability of our failure-tolerant protocol to execute arbitrary programs on a shared channel by showing that it can execute a simple multi-party protocol reliably, securely, and efficiently, even in the presence of up to two malicious agents. This is done by incorporating our protocol as a sub-routine in a larger system that includes additional logic and securely executes tasks such as electronic voting, software update, and executable code distribution. We believe that our failure-tolerant protocol serves as a valuable building block for the secure execution of various tasks on a shared channel with a malicious adversary. We provide the code for our protocol under the MIT license, making it easily modifiable and extensible by other researchers. The proposed protocol results in execution costs of approximately $2.5$ seconds and memory usage of approximately 32 MB for executing a simple program with a input length of 128 KB by $n=10$ cooperating agents. We also successfully execute the protocol with a failure-tolerant feature that includes additional logic for executing a multi-party protocol securely, reliably, and efficiently with up to $k=2$ malicious agents with execution costs of approximately 5 seconds and memory usage of approximately 64 MB for executing a simple program with a input length of 128 KB by $n=5$ cooperating agents. We believe that our failure-tolerant protocol serves as an efficient, secure, and reliable solution for executing tasks on a shared channel with a malicious adversary and paves the way for the secure execution of various tasks that incorporate our protocol as a sub-routine. As a step in optimizing trigger algorithms for future experiments, we develop criteria to select events characterized by multiple photon emissions.  These criteria are established by analyzing the characteristics of subleading photons in deep inelastic scattering processes at the LHC, specifically involving the production of heavy vector bosons.  We demonstrate that events involving the second most energetic photon, with an energy of at least 10 GeV, have minimal losses in acceptance levels of 95% or higher for a range of vector boson masses between 200 and 700 GeV.  We also examine the distribution of the leading photon's rapidity and show that even without selecting on the charge of the vector boson, our criteria yield acceptable levels of misidentification, primarily stemming from proton reconstruction, totaling 10% or less for all rapidity bins.  As for the selection of the second most energetic photon, we establish energy thresholds of 5 GeV for events produced by processes with two photons and 7 GeV for those with three photons.  We further analyze events characterized by three photons and find that our criteria have levels of acceptance of 80% or higher for events involving the production of heavy vector bosons with masses between 200 and 700 GeV.  We emphasize that optimizing trigger algorithms for events involving the production of heavy vector bosons also requires considerations of missing transverse momentum.  As such, we investigate the impact of requiring large values of missing transverse momentum on event acceptance levels.  We find that our criteria yield levels of acceptance of 20% or higher for events with pairs of vector bosons that fire the trigger algorithm for two photons with energies of at least 10 GeV in the rapidity range |0.5| to |2.5|. As the interstellar gas collapses, it transfers metals to forming stars, so the observed elemental abundances in young stars reflect the average metallicity of the interstellar medium from which they formed.  However, as shown in previous research, the relationship is not entirely straightforward due to physical processes occurring within the molecular cloud.  These processes can disperse high-density gas, reducing the metallicity of the gas from which the stars form, thus affecting the observed abundances.  As a result, the metallicity of the interstellar medium is not the sole factor influencing elemental abundances in young stars.  Still, it has a significant impact, and by examining abundances in all elements, both light and heavy, we can recover the average metallicity of the interstellar medium from which they originated.  Using a newly developed model of cloud physics, we simulated the formation of the OMC1 main region, a well-studied source of young stars with well-determined elemental abundances.  By analyzing these abundances, we found that the average metallicity of the interstellar gas that formed the stars as 12 + log10(R) = 8.96 ± 0.13, which is comparable to the metallicity of the interstellar medium in the Milky Way determined from the absorption lines of young stars.  However, our research also highlights the diversity of metallicity in the interstellar gas that formed the stars in the OMC1 main region, with a larger spread than the error margin of our primary estimate, indicating that a significant portion of the spread in elemental abundances in young stars may result from the varying metallicity of the interstellar gas rather than physical processes within the molecular cloud. This study introduces a novel approach to measuring the fault tolerance of a blockchain by focusing on the interconnection of miner accounts. Building on this concept, we developed the Account Interconnection Graph (AIG) model. Key features of AIG include: (a) it provides a clear, compact representation of the relationships between miners; (c) it offers a manageable way to examine the connectivity among all accounts within the blockchain; (b) it paves the way for investigating crucial properties of the blockchain, such as its fault tolerance. By creating a linear layout of the AIG, we can visualize the order in which accounts transact with each other. This allows us to identify specific transactions that shape the future of the blockchain and make it more resilient. In turn, this enables us to design strategies to enhance the fault tolerance of the blockchain. Furthermore, we propose a novel approach to locating the most critical transactions that can provide benefits in various applications, such as securing the blockchain against 51%-attack proofs of work proofs of stake and hybrid consensus protocols. This research provides open-source software for visualizing the AIG and identifying the most critical transactions in the blockchain. It also paves the way for exploring more advanced topics, such as verifying the correctness of strategies designed to enhance the fault tolerance of the blockchain. The findings of this study can be built upon by conducting more in-depth analyses of the AIG in the context of specific blockchain architectures. The AIG model can be applied to any blockchain system, regardless of its size, as long as it is based on account interconnections. This study uses a simplified example of the Bitcoin blockchain to illustrate the AIG model in action. However, scaling the AIG to accommodate the massive transaction history of large blockchains like Bitcoin may be computationally costly. This research proposes an alternative approach called the Linear Decreasing Threshold (LDT) method to efficiently identify the most critical transactions in the blockchain. A key limitation of these measurements is likely to be set by shot-noise constraints when signal powers are minimal.  To overcome this barrier, signals must be amplified through backscattering off a shared mechanical reservoir, reducing the impact of random fluctuations. meeting notes from the session led by
  Tim Berners-Lee on day six of the World Wide Web Project's meeting in
  CERN, where key discussions centered on data format, protocol, and system
  purposes. Notably, he introduced the concept of a Web server, which
  marks a significant deviation from his initial presentation of the
  project, with a focus on providing access to information resources using
  links. During the meeting, discussions also touched on how to use HTML
  links to access different formats of data, the potential benefits of
  linking existing databases, and the possibility of charging fees for
  specific information resources. Additionally, Tim Berners-Lee mentioned
  his willingness to manage the project's system purposes manually, but
  expressed concerns about doing so for a large user base. The meeting
  concluded with decisions to make HTML, HTTP, and CERN's Web server
  technologies freely available, and to establish a non-profit organisation
  to manage the Web, with Tim Berners-Lee as its director.  These notes
  from the meeting also include a detailed outline of future actions. 
  Although CERN ultimately did not end up hosting the Web, with the

Abstract:  This paper discusses the strategy of adjusting the angular orientation of the TianQin space-based gravitational wave detector to minimize noise pollution from the surrounding environment. By simulating the effects of rotation on tidal gravitational waves and modeling the noise sources and the detector's motion, it is possible to determine the optimal orientation that minimizes noise pollution. This paper presents the results of these simulations and the benefits of using this strategy.

This study introduces an all-optical waveguide modulator capable of executing Bragg filtering in the time domain and demonstrates the feasibility of reviving a modulated red optical field within a photonic crystal waveguide using a blue driving light wave. A specific gap in research relates to establishing reliable guidelines for deciding when $l_1$ perturbations affect a model's performance critically. ann-Hilbert problem has a solution for a specific class of functions characterized by growth conditions. In this study, we investigate the existence of a solution for a more general class of functions defined on complex numbers by introducing the concept of "polynomially controlled functions." This class, which includes functions with rates of growth, is examined in relation to the Riemann-Hilbert problem when the number of specified functions is greater than two. Our findings show that when the number of functions exceeds two, the solution depends on the rate of growth and is not determined by properties such as analyticity. This discovery leads to distinguishing between two classes of functions with rates of growth, each requiring a different level of analyticity, resulting in solutions to the Riemann-Hilbert problem that are unique up to additive constants of the matrix-valued function involved. Models of these systems often take the form of nonlinear differential equations, although their traditional analytical solutions are typically derived under the assumption of constant parameters. This research develops a statistical framework for estimating the values of parameters and functions of them that are initially unknown, using data from the systems' state over time. It does so by combining the advantages of numerical methods for solving differential equations and Bayesian statistical analysis. Specifically, it uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations to assess the credibility of parameter value combinations that are based on observed data and simulate the system's response to its past events. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel real-time indoor lighting invariant method, ensuring the robustness of these applications.  Guided by the theory that indoor features remain consistent under different lighting conditions, we employ a two-step approach to achieve invariance.   how neurons with spatially selective responses, typical of some visual areas,
  maintain consistent representations across translations. We used a recently
  introduced metric, the approximate within-class variance, to assess the
  invariance of neurons to translations. Our results showed that many neurons

  where the system first detects local features with low spatial extent, followed
  by the combination of these features into larger structures with varying levels
  of spatial extent and corresponding levels of representation invariance. We
  believe that our data support multiple previous findings and provide a more

In this model, each node has a unique identifier and a distinct label for its connected edges. We investigate two key algorithmic problems in this model: determining the number of nodes, finding the shortest distance to a particular node. For the first problem, we demonstrate an algorithm requiring 6(n,d) messages in a labeled directed graph with n nodes and a maximum directed path length of d. In the first part, we examine the mechanisms and rules governing synaptic plasticity, including spike-time-Dependent-Plasticity (STDP).  We review the key features of STDP, the algorithms that drive it, and the role it plays in learning and filtering.  We also look at recent studies, models, and experiments related to STDP, as well as its implementation in large-scale neural networks.  In the second part, we discuss computational models of schizophrenia. We review recent studies on these models, discussing their implementation, key features, and the role of synaptic plasticity, including STDP, in them.  We also examine recent neuroimaging research on schizophrenia and its underlying neural mechanisms.  We conclude by highlighting the potential of computational models based on STDP for studying schizophrenia and related disorders.  We discuss the models' limitations, propose avenues for further research, and explore their clinical applications. increasing interest in recursive neural network models for their ability to represent complex functions. This study explores the underlying mathematics to demonstrate that a specific recurrent neural network model can be viewed as a weighted sum of its hidden state activations. By applying this insight to a representative model, we establish that it does not utilize the sequence information for a critical period during the optimization process and subsequently leads to poor performance. Furthermore, we identify a condition under which this model's hidden state remains beneficial for a longer period, and provide a mathematical framework to enhance previous findings regarding the relationship between the recurrent neural network's parameters and its performance. Our approach also offers a practical solution to improve the model's performance during the early stages, and paves the way for developing more effective recursive neural network models. Our experiments demonstrate that by employing this proposed model, we can achieve superior results compared to existing methods, and our analysis provides a clearer understanding of the representation learning capabilities of this model. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zwang84/recurrent_network_analysis. The introduction of the High Energy Transient Experiment (HTEX) aboard the International Space Station marks a significant shift, as it represents the first space-based X-ray transient monitor featuring a wide field-of-view and broad energy range. By monitoring the sky two times a day at a sensitivity matching the discovery of the first X-ray transient from a distant source, HTEX has the potential to achieve a comparable level of success. With its capability to detect a billion X-rays per year, HTEX is an integral part of a next-generation transient multi-messenger program alongside the Square Kilometre Array and the eXTP. By complementing the scientific objectives of these facilities in the areas of low-mass X-ray binary research, nuclear processes in the universe, and extreme X-ray phenomena, HTEX is an opportunity that should not be missed. Furthermore, as a transient-focused instrument, HTEX is also well-positioned to make significant contributions to the study of the X-ray transient population from the low-end of active galactic nuclei energy spectrum, in addition to providing critical information for the follow-up of gamma-ray bursts and the transient phenomena associated with supernovae in nearby galaxies. Combining the scientific potential of HTEX with the analytical capabilities of the European Space Agency's Vision 2050 Roadmap provides a framework for future missions that could be developed in the 2030s, with a view to launching HTEX in the late 2020s or the early 2030s. To this end, further development of HTEX is advised, alongside a proposal for a mission concept that could serve as a precursor to a full-scale implementation. With an expected cost of approximately 500 million euros, the proposed configuration of HTEX is capable of achieving a level of success comparable to that achieved with the first X-ray from a distant source, while also paving the way for a full-scale implementation in the late 2020s or the early 2030s. However, due to the significant discrepancy between code development speed and the speed of execution on modern hardware, the ability to easily create high-performance algorithms has become a major obstacle preventing researchers from fully leveraging the power of these computers for symbolic computation. In an effort to resolve this issue and make the performance of {\sc GEM} closer to its potential, we significantly restructured and optimized its core functions, achieving a speed on this specific hardware that is comparable to that of the highly efficient but difficult to use {\sc GiAC} computer algebra system. Furthermore, our experience shows that achieving a 5-fold improvement in code development speed is a more significant challenge than achieving a 5-fold increase in execution speed. By providing the details of our optimization approach, the structure of the algorithms used, and the results obtained, we intend to contribute our knowledge to other researchers who are also working to efficiently utilize modern hardware for symbolic computation, as well as to provide a case study on the effectiveness of different code development methodologies. This research paper focuses on the core quantum NGD algorithm, providing a theoretical foundation for further investigations and more intricate implementations of quantum machine learning applications.   Our research proposes a method to automatically identify difficult examples 
  that are likely to benefit from human labeling, allowing us to focus labeling 
  on the most useful data. 
  We achieve this by creating multiple models that are less accurate but efficient 
  to train, which are used to predict the uncertainty of new, previously unseen 
  data. 
  These models are compared based on their performance, size, and training time, 
  which are calculated using a novel, simple approach that takes into account 
  the ensemble they form. 
  We call this method Ensemble Valuation (EV). 
  EV identifies the ensemble that provides a perfect balance between performance and 
  efficiency, which we use to select the most uncertain data to label. 
  Our experiments show that EV significantly improves the active learning strategy 
  by focusing labeling on the most useful data, which in turn leads to a marked 
  improvement in performance when compared to other, established methods. 
  We also found that EV accurately reflects the difficulty of data even when it is 
  difficult to determine, which facilitates the creation of a precise, tailored 
  active learning strategy. 
  Our approach has implications for using pre-trained models as feature extractors, 
  which is common practice, by evaluating the ensemble of models obtained by 
  fine-tuning the pre-trained model for each candidate. 
  We believe that EV offers significant practical value, which is supported by our 
  findings, as it allows for the simultaneous evaluation of multiple models that 
  are trained differently. 
  Our research provides a clear starting point for exploring methods that select 
  models based on EV, which in turn depends on the application at hand. 
  We have made our code and data available at https://github.com/Active-Learning/Ensemble-Valuation. 
  Our approach has several potential applications in the field of few-shot learning 
  and meta-learning, which involve searching over a vast space of models, as it 
  provides a precise, efficient way to compare them. 
  We also propose a simple, efficient way to compare models based on their 
  performance, which involves calculating the area under the receiving operating 
  curve (AUC-ROC).

  interpret, and provides a precise, numerical value that reflects the performance 
  of each model.

Assemblies of genomic data are prone to errors, contaminated with non-functional elements like transposons, and feature alternative chromosomal arrangements in different species. Based on large-scale mapping of protein-DNA interactions across the genome, we used a computational strategy to predict functional elements in the monkey species M. acrodontus.   high altitudes, MageAIC can achieve improved angular resolution for its detected
  events. To optimize the telescope's imaging performance at high elevations, this
  study uses a simulation-based approach to evaluate the optimal equipment specs
  needed for effective operation. A telescope with a 10-meter diameter mirror is
  simulated at three high-altitude locations - 3300, 4200 and 4900 meters above
  sea level - and the resulting image data is analyzed to determine the optimal
  telescope parameters that minimize angular resolution. To achieve a 1-degree angular
  resolution, the simulations indicate that a telescope with a 10-meter diameter
  mirror is required at elevations of 4200-4900 meters above sea level. However,
  such a setup may have significant technical limitations at high elevations. As an
  alternative, a smaller telescope with a 6.5-meter diameter mirror is also
  simulated at the 4900-meter elevation and is found to achieve a 1.25-degree angular
  resolution, which is still superior to the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) baselines
  for a next-generation gamma-ray observatory.  The optimal MageAIC design can
  be further refined to achieve the desired performance at the chosen elevation.  A
  summary of the key findings along with the theoretical background, design of the
  MageAIC telescope, and the simulation-based approach used in this study are
  presented in the main text.  Additionally, the detailed simulation results for the
  optimal telescope parameters are provided in the appendix.

To improve the efficiency of these methods, this research leverages the fundamental concept of dimensionality reduction in machine learning. A key challenge arises from the lack of transparent derivatives from many safety certification methods, making it difficult to employ dimensionality reduction techniques effectively. To overcome this obstacle, this study introduces two novel, efficient methods for reducing the size of neural networks while maintaining precise safety guarantees. By utilizing the optimization-based method CEGS with envelope, which provides transparent derivatives, we develop an effective way to safely reduce the network's size after obtaining a safety guarantee for the original network. Additionally, we identify an optimal threshold for further efficient network pruning. To illustrate the efficacy of these methods, we use them to safely reduce neural networks in real-world applications, achieving a significant 8-fold increase in model efficiency with only a 2-fold increase in computation cost.   one-way or directional coupling, enables us to control how light is shared

  However, achieving one-way coupling in a full photonic crystal waveguide

  an infinite bandwidth and we show that these waveguides can be realized

  What's more, we show that these waveguides can support a vast number of

  high capacity to transmit light. To validate our theoretical findings,
  we used a process called atomic force microscopy to precisely measure
  the heights of the photonic crystal structures and then used a computational
  method to simulate how light interacts with these structures.
  The results of these simulations revealed that our novel waveguide
  offers the unique benefit of one-way coupling across an infinite bandwidth.

This concept can be extended to certain functions $f$ that are invariant under certain permutations. For $f$ to be a distinct part function of order $k$, it must satisfy conditions related to moments and polynomial properties. This paper explores specific functions $f$ that meet these criteria for $k$ values greater than 2 and provides related conjectures. Notably, we prove the uniqueness of functions that are sums of products of distinct pairs for $k = 3$ and $k = 4$, which are equivalent to the Herding Linear Program's solutions for these $k$ values. Additionally, we discuss a new method for encoding the permutation-invariant properties of the $k$-th moment polynomial using the distinct part functions of order $k$. This method is analogous to the method used in the original paper by Speyer and Diaconis but is more comprehensive and provides the foundation for further research.   We have tested VEGE on a range of scenes, from indoor to outdoor settings, and observed a 
  significant improvement in lighting realism with only a minimal increase in memory requirements. 
  Environment maps generated with VEGE can be easily shared and used across different video game 
  engines and applications, also serving as a useful tool for artists in need of completed 
  radiance data. 
  To facilitate widespread adoption, we are making the VEGE source code and environment maps 
  publicly available under a permissive license. 
  Compared to other global illumination methods, VEGE offers an appealing blend of lighting 
  realism, easy implementation, and low memory requirements, all of which are highly desirable 
  features in the video game industry. 
  We have achieved this result with VEGE by utilizing a compact representation that includes 
  both exposure values and completed radiance data. 
  This representation provides a solid foundation for applying more advanced post-processing 
  effects while still meeting the industry's speed and memory requirements. 
  To further demonstrate the flexibility and versatility of VEGE, we have experimented with 
  combining it with other screen space ambient occlusion techniques. 
  The code for VEGE has been integrated into the Unreal Engine as a plugin under the name 
  'Vege', also serving as a starting point for users who wish to tailor the method to their 
  specific needs. 
  To facilitate real-world applications, we have established a workflow that includes VEGE, 
  which we believe is applicable to not only the video game industry but also film visual effects 
  and other fields that involve the creation of high dynamic range images. 
  This workflow, in turn, is built upon a two-step exposure bracketing technique that we have 
  also found valuable on its own right.
